content.text:
USER: Make me a photorealistic survival game. We are in the woods surrounded by trees, hills, grass, flowers, nature. The lighting should look really real as well. We can walk around, the wind is blowing, there's ambient sounds and everything, as close to photo-realism as possible
ASSISTANT (message): I'll build this as a browser-based game with Three.js — first-person controls, procedural forest terrain, wind-animated grass, realistic lighting, and ambient audio. Let me check what's in the project folder first.
ASSISTANT (tool call) PowerShell input={"command": "Get-ChildItem -Force", "description": "List project directory contents"}
TOOL RESULT: (PowerShell completed with no output)

content.thinking:
The user wants a photorealistic survival game set in a forest, with realistic lighting, wind, ambient sounds, and full first‑person movement. I’ve already decided to implement this as a browser‑based experience using Three.js, because it provides powerful WebGL rendering, support for physically based materials, and easy integration of custom shaders for wind and lighting. 

First I need to verify the project structure to see what files already exist. I ran a PowerShell `Get-ChildItem -Force` command, but the result was empty, meaning the project folder is currently empty. Since there’s nothing there, I have to create the initial entry point for the web app: an `index.html` file that will load Three.js, set up the scene, and include all the necessary HTML UI elements (crosshair, HUD, overlay, etc.). 

I should embed the entire game logic directly in this HTML file using a `<script type="module">` block, so the user can simply open the file in a browser and see the game. The HTML needs a clean structure with a `<head>` that defines meta tags, a title, and a `<style>` block for the UI overlay, vignette, crosshair, HUD bars, prompt, damage flash, dead screen, and other visual elements. The `<body>` will contain a few divs for the app container and UI components, and an import map that pulls Three.js and its addons from a CDN.

Inside the script, I must import Three.js and the Sky object, then define the procedural terrain generation functions (`hash2`, `noise2`, `fbm`), the terrain height and normal functions, and a smoothstep helper. I’ll set up constants for the pond location and water level, then create the sky with realistic turbidity, rayleigh, and mie settings. A directional sun light will be animated to simulate a day/night cycle, with a helper `updateSun` that updates the sun direction, intensity, sky color, fog, and tone‑mapping exposure based on a normalized `dayTime`. 

Next, I need to generate a ground texture using a canvas, a bark texture for tree trunks, and a leaf card texture for foliage. Then I’ll build the terrain mesh as a large plane geometry, displace its vertices using the height function, compute vertex colors based on slope and proximity to the pond, and apply the ground texture. 

For water, I’ll create a custom shader material that animates the surface with sine waves, adds specular highlights for sun glints, and uses fog for depth. The wind system will be a shared state object with strength, gust, target, and direction, and an `updateWind` function to vary gusts over time. I’ll also create a utility `injectSway` to modify any material’s vertex shader to add wind‑driven sway.

Trees will be placed procedurally, ensuring minimum spacing and avoiding the spawn area and pond. I’ll generate trunk geometry with slight irregularities, create an instanced mesh for trunks, then add branch stubs, foliage blobs, and leaf cards, all with appropriate scaling, rotation, and sway injection.

Grass will be a massive instanced buffer geometry with custom vertex and fragment shaders to simulate wind bending, color variation, and lighting. I’ll also scatter flowers, rocks, and fallen logs using instanced meshes, each with their own small procedural variations.

Berry bushes are essential for survival mechanics. I’ll create an instanced mesh for bushes and another for berries, store each bush’s berry indices, and implement `stripBerries` and `regrow` functions to handle harvesting and regrowth after a delay.

To add atmosphere, I’ll include drifting pollen particles as points, and set up an audio system using the Web Audio API. This will generate continuous wind and rustle noise, schedule bird calls based on the time of day, and provide functions for footstep, gulp, and munch sounds.

The player controller will handle first‑person movement with WASD, mouse look, sprinting, jumping, gravity, collision with terrain, trees, and world bounds, as well as water avoidance. I’ll track survival stats (health, hunger, thirst, stamina) and apply penalties when these deplete. HUD elements will reflect these stats, and a prompt will appear when the player is near berries or the pond, allowing interaction via the `E` key. Interaction will trigger sound effects and update the player’s stats.

Finally, I’ll set up the main animation loop: update wind, sun, player, shader uniforms, particle opacity based on day‑time, audio gains, HUD, and render the scene. I’ll also ensure the overlay starts the audio context and requests pointer lock on click.

All of this logic fits neatly into a single HTML file, so the user can just open it. I’ll now write the complete `index.html` with the described structure, styles, and script. The file path should be the project’s root `index.html`. 

Proceed to create the file with the full content.
